passages.text: The question: What is knowledge, who is the knower, and what is it that one can know? How are these concepts grounded in experience, and how does the Co-existentialism of Shri A. Nagraj compare with Advaita Vedanta, modern Western philosophy, and the natural sciences?

This study examines knowledge, the knower, and the knowable in Madhyasth Darshan (Co-existentialism), as presented by Shri A. Nagraj, and compares its answers with Advaita Vedanta and modern science and philosophy.

The Ontology of Coexistence supplies the ontological setting: Omnipresence, saturated units, the four orders, constitutional completeness, and the active structure of jeevan. The present study asks the specifically epistemological questions the primary texts develop: what knowledge is, what makes jeevan the knower, how coexistence becomes the known, and why understanding must become evident in action, relationship, evaluation, and humane tradition. From Unit Activity to Human Orderliness is used as an interpretive audit of these connections, not as a primary source and not as a source of notation for this paper.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan Answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan approaches knowledge through a practical question: how does understanding reality enable human beings to live without contradiction? Complete knowledge is neither accumulated information nor detached speculation. It is the realized understanding of reality as coexistence, of the conscious self (jeevan), and of humane conduct. The knower is jeevan, while an embodied human being—jeevan and physical body together—expresses and validates that understanding in daily life. What is known is existence itself: the eternal coexistence of all-pervasive Omnipresence and active units across four orders of nature. Knowing begins in reflective study, guides choices before action, manifests in behavior and productive work, and returns to the knower through evaluation. Knowing is completed only when it becomes evident in living.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 Knowledge, knower, and known

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Complete knowledge (sampurna gyan) comprises three canonical, inseparable domains (KD §3.5, p. 69; KD §3.17, pp. 145–150; JV, p. 40; SB, p. 116):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge of Existence as Coexistence (Astitva Darshan Gyan): Understanding reality as the eternal coexistence of all-pervasive Omnipresence (vyapak satta) and countless active units of nature (prakriti).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge of the Conscious Self (Jeevan Gyan): Understanding the constitution, faculties, ten activities, and potential for awakening of the conscious unit (jeevan).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge of Humane Conduct (Manaviyata Purna Acharan Gyan): Understanding the values, character, ethics, and orderliness through which awakened human beings live and participate in existence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Some primary passages enumerate four constituents by listing participation in overall orderliness beside these three (KD §3.5, p. 69). Participation is the living field in which the three become manifest, rather than a detached, separate reality. Knowledge is therefore not an abstract mental representation of an external world. What exists, who knows it, how the knower conducts human life, and how that conduct fulfills universal order belong together as a single, coherent whole.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The word gyan also carries a foundational ontological meaning: it names the ever-present, all-pervasive ground in which all units exist (MVD, pp. 34–35). In this sense, Space (Avakash), Omnipresence (Vyapak Satta), and Knowledge (Gyan) refer to the same reality. Ontological Knowledge is actionless (kriya-heen) and non-transforming (aparinami): it is neither an activity nor an agent performing actions, yet it serves as the tranquil ground, energy source, and inspiration for all active units. All units are active. Sentience belongs to jeevan, not to insentient nature or to the formless space in which all units are immersed (MVD, pp. 11, 32–33). Saturated in Omnipresence, nature is coexistence itself, orderly, intelligible, and available for direct realization.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The universal availability of knowledge follows from the nature of human life and the shared constitution of jeevan. Happiness is the inseparable innate nature (dharma) of human beings, and knowledge is its foundation (MVD, p. 115). Every person inherently yearns for happiness, but genuine happiness requires living without internal contradiction—which is possible only through understanding reality as it is. Furthermore, all human beings possess an identical conscious constitution: the strengths and powers of jeevan are the same in everyone, and every jeevan shares the equal capacity to understand existence and to evidence coexistence (JV, pp. 33–34, 44). Differences in present understanding reflect prior impressions (sanskar), environment, and education, not an unequal innate capacity.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge is ever-present throughout coexistence; it unfolds in realization by jeevan and becomes evident in living conduct and expression (MVD, pp. 35, 115–116, 289). Jeevan is the bearer of realization, comprehension, contemplation, deliberation, and selection. Yet a living person carries the proof through understanding and conduct: an embodied human being speaks, works, relates, evaluates, teaches, and builds tradition. Jeevan knows; the human being presents its living evidence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: An awakened human experiences the omnipresent ground across four aspects of living: as law (niyam) in work, resolution (samadhan) in thought, bliss (anand) in realization, and justice (nyaya) in behavior (MVD, p. 34). Each term identifies a definite dimension of life. Realized knowledge dissolves internal contradiction, establishing resolution in thought, lawful productive work, just relationships, and harmonious participation in the world.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The known (gyeya) is existence as coexistence. It encompasses nature across its four orders (material, plant, animal, and human knowledge order) saturated in Omnipresence. Madhyasth Darshan defines what is known across three aspects of Truth (Satya) (YAT; MVD, pp. 88, 97):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Inherent Truth (Vastugat Satya): The reality of each unit’s bounded form (roop), relative properties (guna), natural usefulness or essential nature (svabhav), and inseparable innateness (dharma).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Positional / Relational Truth (Vastu-sthiti Satya): The situational, ecological, and temporal reality of units—their direction, time, place, and mutual complementariness in the order of nature.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Existential Truth (Sthiti Satya): Existential reality unaffected by time—nature (both insentient and sentient) saturated in all-pervasive Omnipresence, which is coexistence itself.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Measuring physical properties with instruments is only one limited aspect of knowing. Physical, intellectual, and coexistential knowledge are distinguished, expressed through practical skill, professional proficiency, and philosophical wisdom (KD, pp. 3–4). The scope of the known extends into production and ecology: human freedom must protect and rightly use natural abundance rather than disrupt the cyclic balance of the other orders (SB, pp. 111, 121, 149).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The known becomes fully meaningful when awakening fulfills human aspiration through undivided society and universal orderliness (KD §3.17, p. 148). Coexistence is what is known; living with resolution, prosperity, mutual trust, and harmony proves that knowledge has become a living reality. The world does not lose its reality when understood: nature is perpetual (shashwat) rather than an illusion cancelled by enlightenment (MVD, pp. 12–13).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Shri A. Nagraj’s inquiry began by examining two historical approaches to these questions (KD §3.17, pp. 146–147). Mystical and idealist traditions often treated the world as an illusion or an ineffable divine mystery, leaving human life dependent on supernatural intervention. Materialism, conversely, attempted to derive consciousness from physical compositions of matter, struggling to explain purpose, values, or subjective experience. Neither framework provided a coherent foundation for universal human conduct. Madhyasth Darshan grounds epistemology in the conscious jeevan and its living evidence in the world.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Beside knowledge, knower, and known, the primary texts articulate several parallel operational triads that keep knowing rooted in active human life (KD §3.17, pp. 145–150; §3.18, pp. 151–152). These include coexistential vision, seer jeevan, and the scene of coexistence (darshan–drish–drishya); focused attention, the human attender, and the goal of awakening (dhyan–dhyata–dhyeya); coexistence as cause, jeevan as conscious doer, and humane living as effect (karan–karta–karya); awakening as aim, the human as seeker, and the joint form of jeevan and body as means (sadhya–sadhak–sadhan); and seer, doer, and enjoyer (drishta–karta–bhokta). In physical nature, units act as self-motivated doers; in animal life, animals act as doers and enjoyers driven by instinct without understanding. In the awakened human, understanding establishes true seer-status (drishta-pad), illuminating action so that the human acts as a conscious, righteous doer and experiences enduring fulfillment as the enjoyer.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The conscious knower (jeevan) is constitutionally complete (gathan-purna). Because its atomic constitution neither admits nor expels constituent particles, it does not decompose or decay, persisting across bodily birth and death (JV, pp. 19, 36). Its evidential standing is examined further in §7.4.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 Why knowledge matters: awakening and the human goal

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge is indispensable because human beings belong to the knowledge order (gyan avastha). Unlike material units that follow physical laws, plants that follow seed-conformance (beej-anushangita), and animals that follow breed-conformance (vanshanushangita), human conduct is governed by culture and understanding (sanskar-anushangita). Human beings possess imagination (kalpanasheelta) and freedom of action (karm-swatantrata). Their conduct is not biologically programmed. When humans choose and act without understanding, they adopt contradictory assumptions, generate conflict, and disrupt their natural environment. Knowledge is required to align human freedom with the harmony of coexistence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The immediate epistemic goal is freedom from delusion (bhram-mukti) and comprehensive resolution (samadhan). Delusion begins when the perishable body is mistaken for the self, and continuous happiness is sought through temporary sensory gratification (indriya-sukh). Bodily needs for food, rest, protection, and procreation are legitimate and necessary for physical survival, but they are temporary and recurring; they cannot satisfy jeevan’s conscious yearning for continuous happiness. Resolution is comprehensive understanding that provides clear, unambiguous answers to “why and how” across all human activities (MVD, pp. 34, 312). Awakening (jagriti) is the state in which inward reflection reaches genuine understanding, and that understanding consistently governs thought, choice, speech, behavior, and work.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The four internal values of jeevan (jeevan mulya) describe the progressive harmony experienced in mental well-being (manah-swasthata): happiness (sukh), peace (shanti), contentment (santosh), and bliss (anand) (MVD, pp. 207–208; JV, p. 137). Each represents the internal satisfaction that arises when lower faculties are guided by higher ones (§1.3). Distinct from these four inter-faculty harmonies, Supreme Bliss (Paramanand) is experienced when atma abides in unbroken concurrence with all-pervasive Omnipresence upon realization (MVD, pp. 208, 327). Material wealth cannot substitute for unresolved understanding, nor can private emotional calm replace just relationships.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These internal harmonies become complete when joined with the fourfold Human Goal (Manav Lakshya) (KD §3.17, p. 150; JV, pp. 60, 165):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Resolution (Samadhan) in every individual: Intellectual clarity free from doubt and contradiction.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Prosperity (Samriddhi) in every family: The assured production and availability of physical goods in excess of genuine family needs, rooted in right use rather than endless accumulation.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Fearlessness and Mutual Trust (Abhay) in society: Social relationships governed by justice, trust, and mutual respect, free from exploitation and fear of aggression.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Coexistence (Saha-astitva) in nature and universal order: Harmonious, non-destructive participation in the ecological balance of nature and universal human order.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These goals form a continuous, cumulative chain: individual resolution fosters family prosperity; prosperity supports social fearlessness and trust; and mutual trust enables universal coexistence. Resolution brings happiness; resolution with prosperity brings peace; the addition of societal trust brings contentment; and living in universal coexistence brings bliss (KD, p. 112). Epistemic clarity, material sufficiency, relational justice, and ecological balance reinforce one another without trade-offs.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: To achieve this movement, Madhyasth Darshan distinguishes three connected functions of understanding (MVD, p. 170):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge (Gyan): Realized understanding of coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Wisdom (Vivek): Discernment of the human goal and universal purpose, distinguishing perishable bodily needs from conscious needs of jeevan.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Science (Vigyan): Determines how material prosperity and the human and jeevan goals can be achieved in harmony with existence (MVD, p. 170).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: When science is separated from knowledge and wisdom, it degenerates into consumerism, environmental devastation, and destructive technologies. Guided by wisdom and knowledge, science ensures sustainable production, ecological regeneration, and the material foundations of peace.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This developmental journey involves three distinct completions (purnata):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Constitutional Completeness (Gathan-purnata): The physical-chemical atom reaches a stable constitution that neither gains nor loses constituent particles, becoming the conscious unit (jeevan). Every jeevan already possesses this constitutional completeness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Activity Completeness (Kriya-purnata): The awakening of all ten activities of jeevan, in which internal effort reaches restfulness (shram ka vishram) and understanding is no longer fragmented by delusion.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Conduct Completeness (Acharan-purnata): The unwavering, living expression of awakened understanding in values, character, ethics, and universal orderliness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 Jeevan, body, and the activities of knowing

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The active knower is jeevan, a constitutionally complete sentient unit whose ten activities are organized across five concentric faculties (JV, pp. 72–73, 91, 92–93):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Atma (Core / Center): Inward realization (anubhav) and outward authenticity (pramanikta). Situated at the center, it is inherently mediative (madhyasth), free from partisan attractions and repulsions (MVD, p. 211).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Buddhi (Intellect): Inward comprehension (bodh) and outward truth-bearing resolve (ritambhara or sankalpa).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Chitta (Contemplation and Imaging): Inward contemplation (chintan) and outward imaging (chitran). Its receptive activity is direct recognition (sakshatkar) of reality and meaning.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Vritti (Thought / Deliberation): Inward deliberation (tulan) and outward analysis (vishleshan).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Mun (Mind / Sensory Interface): Inward tasting (aswadan) and outward selection (chayan).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These ten activities divide functionally into five inward-looking forces of state (bal)—tasting, deliberation, contemplation, comprehension, realization—and five outward-looking powers of motion (shakti)—selection, analysis, imaging/desire, resolve, and authenticity (KD §3.6, pp. 70–71). In human life, these five powers manifest as hope (asha at mun), thought (vichar at vritti), desire (ichha at chitta), truth-resolve (ritambhara at buddhi), and authenticity (pramanikta at atma) (KD §3.16, p. 145; MVD, p. 83).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: When the faculties work in harmony, with each higher faculty guiding the one below it, these relationships yield the four internal values of jeevan (jeevan mulya) (MVD, pp. 207–208; JV, p. 137):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Happiness (Sukh): Experienced when tasting and selection in the mind (mun) accord with thoughtful deliberation (vritti).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Peace (Shanti): Experienced when deliberation and thought (vritti) accord with the clarity and values of contemplation (chitta).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Contentment (Santosh): Experienced when contemplation and imaging (chitta) accord with intellectual comprehension (buddhi).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Bliss (Anand): Experienced when intellectual comprehension (buddhi) accords with existential realization in atma.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These activities operate in two coordinated directions:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Inward Reflection (Pratyavartan): The movement in which sensory impressions, behavior, thoughts, and desires are examined inward toward direct recognition (sakshatkar), intellectual comprehension (bodh), and existential realization (anubhav).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Outward Projection (Paravartan): The movement in which realized understanding and resolve flow outward as harmonious desires, precise analysis, wholesome selection, speech, bodily action, behavior, and social participation (KD §§3.12, 3.16–3.17).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The physical body is essential for presenting evidence, but it is not the knower. The brain (medhas) is the physical organ that receives and processes signals transmitted by jeevan, translating thoughts, desires, and resolves into neural and motor actions (MVD, pp. 83, 200). The body functions under the direction of jeevan, not vice versa (KD §3.16, pp. 141, 143).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The interaction between jeevan and body is defined through the balance of sensitivity and cognisance:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Sensitivity (Sanvedansheelta): Physical responsiveness mediated by the senses (sound, touch, sight, taste, and smell). Sensory contact is vital for bodily survival, but sensations are fleeting and cannot satisfy jeevan’s yearning for continuous happiness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Cognisance (Sangyansheelta): The conscious capacity of jeevan to understand relationships, values, purpose, justice, and existential order.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In an unawakened human, life is dominated by sensitivity: the person chases temporary sensory pleasures, confuses bodily comfort with happiness, and becomes reactive. In an awakened human, cognisance regulates sensitivity: the senses are kept healthy and purposeful, while understanding guides desires and actions (SB, p. 64).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the state of delusion, activity is effective only up to four and a half activities (JV, pp. 72–74; KD §3.17, p. 147): selection and tasting in mun (2), analysis in vritti (1), imaging in chitta (1), and half of comparison in vritti (0.5). That “half” refers to comparison restricted to sensory pleasure, bodily health, and material profit. Contemplation, comprehension, and realization are not yet active as governing guides, and justice, dharma, and truth are not yet the governing criteria.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Awakening does not add a new organ or abolish the senses; it activates the full depth of the faculties. Direction of guidance distinguishes the two states (MVD, pp. 207–208):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Higher-conformance (Purvanukram, पूर्वानुक्रम): Guidance flowing from the faculties antecedent to mun (vritti, chitta, buddhi, atma). Inspiration descends from realization in atma through buddhi, chitta, and vritti down to mun, ensuring that desires and selections are aligned with justice, dharma, and truth.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Lower-conformance (Paranukram, परानुक्रम): Pressure pushing inward from bodily sensations, sensory cravings, and social conditioning, subjecting mun to external compulsions and reducing jeevan to a servant of bodily impulses.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 Practical judgment and humane order

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Humane conduct becomes operational across four connected fields of human activity: bodily propensities, sensory interfaces, social motives, and higher-human beneficence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The Four Bodily Propensities (Vishayas): Food/nourishment (ahar), rest/sleep (nidra), defense/fear (bhaya), and procreation (maithun) (MVD, p. 58). These propensities are shared with animal life and are necessary for physical survival. Understanding regulates them so that they serve life rather than dominate it.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The Five Sensory Modalities: Sound (shabda), touch (sparsha), visible form (roop), taste (rasa), and smell (gandha) (MVD, p. 65). These are the sensory channels through which bodily interactions occur.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The Three Social Motives (Eshanas) and Resolution: Intellectual and social satisfaction is fulfilled through resolution (samadhan) and three humane motives (MVD, pp. 64–65): Vitteshana (Wealth / Prosperity motive): The desire for wealth acquired through righteous labor and justice, directed toward family sufficiency and right use, rather than blind accumulation. Putreshana (Progeny motive): The dedication to nurturing, educating, and continuing future generations in family and social orderliness. Lokeshana (Social Recognition motive): The aspiration to contribute meaningfully to undivided society and universal order, earning trust through service.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Beneficence (Upakar): Altruistic contribution (MVD, p. 73). Deploying one’s physical, intellectual, and material resources to assist others in attaining prosperity and awakening, strengthening their autonomy rather than creating dependency.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Before acting, jeevan deliberates through six evaluative perspectives (drishti) within comparison (tulan in vritti) (MVD, pp. 66–67; JV, pp. 93–98, 139):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Pleasant / Unpleasant (Priya–Apriya): Evaluates immediate sensory comfort and taste.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Healthful / Harmful (Hita–Ahita): Evaluates bodily nutrition, protection, and physical well-being.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Profitable / Unprofitable (Labha–Alabha): Evaluates material exchange, resources, and gain.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Just / Unjust (Nyaya–Anyaya): Evaluates fairness, mutual fulfillment, and values in human relationships.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Orderly / Disorderly (Dharma–Adharma): Evaluates whether action sustains all-round resolution and participation in universal harmony.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: True / Untrue (Satya–Asatya): Evaluates whether understanding accords with existential reality in coexistence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The first three perspectives (priya, hita, labha) are relative and temporary (anitya). Pleasantness, health, and profit provide useful practical information, but they cannot serve as ultimate standards for living. The second three perspectives (nyaya, dharma, satya) are universal and unchanging (nitya) (MVD, p. 212). Awakened conduct is governed by nyaya–dharma–satya, where pleasure, bodily well-being, and material utility are guided and harmonized by justice, resolution, and truth.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Consider a family’s decision about food. Taste, bodily health, and cost all matter. Understanding also asks whether the food was obtained fairly, whether family members’ genuine needs are met, and whether its production damages the conditions of future life. After acting, the family checks the result. A meal may be pleasant yet insufficiently nourishing, or inexpensive because someone else’s labor was undervalued. Evaluation reveals what needs correction in the next decision.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This moral order reflects the cosmic order of nature. In the physical and ecological world, nature operates through law (niyam), regulation (niyantran), and balance (santulan) (MVD, pp. 70–71). Units maintain dynamic balance in mutuality within the all-pervasive ground. Law regulates activity and sustains balance. In human life, balanced living is expressed as justice, and just participation in the larger order as dharma or resolution. Realization in coexistence completes this understanding in truth (MVD, pp. 137, 174).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Humane conduct (manaviyata purna acharan) is structured into three concrete pillars (KD §3.4, p. 67; MVD, p. 35):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Values (Mulya): Recognizing relationships, fulfilling established values (such as trust, respect, affection, care, and gratitude), evaluating the outcome, and achieving mutual satisfaction (ubhay-trupti).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Character (Charitra): Righteous wealth acquired through productive labor (swadhana), fidelity in marital relationships (swadari / swapurusha), and compassionate behavior and work (dayapurna karya-vyavahar).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Ethics (Neeti): The protection and right use of body, mind, and material resources across personal ethics (dharma neeti), economic ethics (artha neeti), and social/political governance (rajya neeti).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This understanding is lived across the four dimensions of human existence: realization (anubhav), thought (vichar), behavior (vyavahar), and productive work (karya). These dimensions express themselves in five universal societal systems (sarvabhaum vyavastha): Education and Culture (Shiksha-Sanskar), Health and Restraint (Swasthya-Samyama), Production and Work (Utpadan-Karya), Exchange and Storage (Vinimaya-Kosh), and Justice and Protection (Nyaya-Suraksha). Epistemology thus directly culminates in universal human orderliness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.5 Knowing, action, and evaluation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In Madhyasth Darshan, the cognitive process is an integrated fourfold progression that defines how units interact with reality (JV, p. 165; MVD, pp. 12, 61–62):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowing (Janna): Directly comprehending the reality of units—their form, properties, essential nature, dharma, and coexistence in Omnipresence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Accepting / Believing (Maanna): Integrating what is known into firm conviction and acceptance, establishing it as the unwavering basis for thought and life.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Recognizing (Pahachanna): Accurately identifying relationships, values, and responsibilities in every encounter.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Fulfilling (Nirvaha Karna): Carrying out those recognized relationships and values through tangible conduct, work, and care.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This progression clarifies the essential difference among the orders of nature:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the material and plant orders, units recognize (pahachanna) and fulfill (nirvaha karna) chemical affinities and biological growth with complete certainty, governed by inherent natural laws.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the animal order, animals recognize and fulfill their interactions guided by bodily instinct and breed-conformance (vanshanushangita).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the unawakened human, a critical breakdown occurs: humans possess imagination and freedom of action, but attempt to accept beliefs (maanna) without knowing reality (janna). Living by unexamined assumptions, dogmas, and sensory conditioning leads to faulty recognition of relationships, unfulfilling actions, conflict, and suffering.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the awakened human, the chain is restored to its natural order: knowing (janna) grounds accepting (maanna), which ensures right recognition (pahachanna) and right fulfillment (nirvaha karna). The discipline of awakening is therefore stated as believing what is known, and knowing what is believed (jo jana hai use manna, jo mana hai use janna) (MVD, p. 12).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A proposal presented for examination (prastav) is distinct from acceptance grounded in realization. A student provisionally entertains the proposal to test it in reflection and practice; only when verified does it become firm conviction grounded in knowledge.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Activity conjoined with aspiration is karma, and every action produces definite consequences. Intentional activity is analyzed through the doer (karta), cause (karan), objective (uddeshya), result (phal), and final effect (parinam) (KD Ch. 1, pp. 2–4). An unawakened human is free when choosing an action, but becomes bound by its ensuing consequences (karm karne me swatantra, phal bhogne me partantra). An awakened human, understanding the lawful order and purpose of coexistence, chooses actions whose intent, values, and relational effects accord with reality; such a person remains free both in action and in experiencing the fruit (phal bhogne me bhi swatantra).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Consequences return to the knower through evaluation (mulyankan). In human relationships, justice is realized through a four-phase cycle (MVD, pp. 310–311; JV, p. 54):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Recognition of Relationship⟶Fulfilment of Values⟶Evaluation⟶Mutual Satisfaction (ubhay-trupti)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Evaluation is not an external score assigned after conduct ends. It is the continuous self-awareness that examines whether the relationship was rightly recognized, whether appropriate values were expressed, whether adequate means were deployed, and whether both parties attained mutual fulfillment.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Evaluation can succeed or fail in four distinct ways:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Right Evaluation (Samyak-mulyankan): Accurately assessing capacity, relationship, need, and result as they truly are.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Over-evaluation (Ati-mulyankan): Attributing greater capacity, value, or fulfillment than is actually present.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Under-evaluation (Av-mulyankan): Failing to recognize the genuine value, effort, or capacity that exists.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Mis-evaluation (Mithya-mulyankan): Applying an erroneous, distorted, or irrelevant criterion altogether (e.g., evaluating a human being by wealth rather than character).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Accurate evaluation shows where understanding, skill, or resources were insufficient, allowing the knower to correct mistakes. What is learned guides the next action. Repeated evaluation, practice, and reflection cultivate sanskar: acceptances, understanding, and tendencies directed toward completeness, which guide subsequent thought and living (MVD, pp. 90, 187, 290). The texts distinguish this cultivation (susanskar) from tendencies shaped by delusion (kusanskar) (MVD, p. 315). Sanskar is not formed in isolation; it develops through interaction with family, teachers, cultural environment, and reflective labor. When a learner is guided by teachers who embody humane values, lived relationships provide tangible models for right recognition. Through sustained personal reflection and behavioral practice, unexamined assumptions and sensory conditioning are gradually replaced by convictions grounded in existential reality. False learning (avidya or agyan) is the failure to understand a reality’s form, properties, essential nature, and dharma as they truly are (MVD, pp. 184, 263–264). True awakening requires consistency across knowing, believing, recognizing, fulfilling, and evaluating.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.6 Evidence, study, and transmission

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan formulates its evidence chain as a living continuity (MVD, pp. 11–12):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Realisation – Behaviour – Experiment. Realisation itself is the ultimate evidence, Evidence itself is the understanding or knowledge, Understanding itself is manifest, The manifest itself is resolution, work and behaviour, Work and behaviour itself is evidence, Evidence itself is awakened tradition, Awakened tradition itself is coexistence.” — MVD, p. 12

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This evidence operates across three inseparable levels (tri-vidha pramana) (MVD, pp. 11–12; SB, p. 44):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Experiential Evidence (Anubhavatmak Pramana): Inward verification in jeevan—the unshakeable realization of coexistence, freedom from doubt, and the stable presence of resolution and peace.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Behavioral Evidence (Vyavaharatmak Pramana): Relational verification in society—just conduct in human relationships that produces mutual satisfaction (ubhay-trupti) and trust.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Experimental / Practical Evidence (Prayogatmak Pramana): Practical verification in nature—work, production, and experimentation that utilize physical and natural laws cyclically and sustainably, generating material prosperity without ecological damage.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This framework reinterprets the classical Indian concept of proof (pramana). Shri A. Nagraj’s founding inquiry questioned whether ultimate proof resides in the written word or its living bearer, in an authoritative scripture or the person who enunciates it (KD, Alternative, point 10). Madhyasth Darshan establishes that a living person carries the proof through understanding and conduct (pramanik vyakti), not the recorded text or formal syllogism alone.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In Manav Karm Darshan (KD, pp. 20–21), apprehension is analyzed through direct perception (pratyaksha), inference (anuman), and testimony-activity (agama-kriya). Direct perception is the realization of continuous proximity; inference is recognizing the possibility of such continuity; and testimony-activity concerns existence beyond what immediate proximity alone can establish. Apprehension operates across gross (sthoola), subtle (sookshma), and causal (karan) levels, engaging ordinary, special, and particular intellectual capacities (samanya, vishesh, vishisht buddhi): gross apprehension grasps form and properties (roop and guna); subtle apprehension grasps properties and essential nature (guna and swabhav); and causal apprehension grasps essential nature and dharma (swabhav and dharma).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nagraj’s autobiographical account records that years of traditional samadhi successfully quieted hopes, thoughts, and desires, but left the unknown still unknown; it was through samyama that the direct perception of reality as coexistence occurred (KD, Alternative, points 1, 5, and 11). He presented the resulting philosophy not as a personal dogma or divine revelation, but as a testable proposal (prastav) for systematic study and verification.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: For learners, the transition from delusion to awakening proceeds through three broad phases: study (adhyayan), experiment and practice (prayog and abhyas), and realization with evidence (anubhav-praman) (MVD, p. 88). This process distinguishes two stages of understanding (MVD, pp. 98–99):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Realization-oriented understanding (Anubhav-gami bodh): The learner’s stage, in which teaching by a guide who embodies understanding enables the student to reflect, attain direct recognition (sakshatkar) of reality in chitta, and accept justice, dharma, and truth in buddhi.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Realization-based understanding (Anubhav-mulak bodh): The awakened stage, in which realization of coexistence in atma flows outward into continuous resolve, contemplation, thought, behavior, and social transmission.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The educational relationship connects the teacher’s living expression with the student’s reflective inquiry (KD, pp. 112–113). The proposal is received through attentive listening and reading (shravan), followed by reflective inquiry (manan). The human thirst for understanding gives this inquiry its starting point (MVD, p. 88). Natural Acceptance (sahaj swikriti) here names this aspiration to understand and live harmoniously. The learner examines the proposal through reasoning, practice, and verification in living.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Verification requires threefold practice (abhyas) (MVD, pp. 143–144):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Literature-practice (Shastra-abhyas): Systematically studying definitions, principles, and holistic concepts to clarify meaning.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Behavioral practice (Vyavahara-abhyas): Applying justice and values in daily family and social relationships to verify mutual satisfaction.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Work practice (Karma-abhyas): Engaging in productive labor with nature to experience physical laws and generate family prosperity.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Through study and practice, the meaning behind words becomes directly recognized (sakshatkar) in chitta, leading to intellectual comprehension (bodh) in buddhi, direct realization of coexistence (anubhav) in atma, and living authenticity (pramanikta).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Transmission is essential because knowledge is claimed to be universally accessible, not an ineffable private secret. Understanding is proven by the ability to convey it clearly to others without contradiction (JV, p. 25). The learner must be able to explain the philosophy, live it in relationships, evaluate its results, and help establish an awakened cultural tradition (jagrit parampara).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: What prevents realization is mystery (rahasyata)—the inability to understand, explain, or demonstrate reality (MVD, p. 209). Primary texts specifically define intellectual mystery (bauddhik rahasyata) as the internal misalignment and contradiction among the faculties of jeevan—when mun does not find refuge in vritti, vritti in chitta, or chitta in buddhi (MVD, p. 279). Intellectual mystery is resolved through exploration (anushandhan)—the original, inventive inquiry accomplished by Nagraj—and through systematic study, emulation, and practice (adhyayan, anukaran, abhyas) within an awakened tradition (MVD, pp. 279–282).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The commitment of Madhyasth Darshan is to universal knowability (sarva-gyeyata): the fundamental structure of coexistence, the conscious self, and humane conduct can be fully known, understood, lived, and taught without ontological mystery (MVD, p. 317). Universal knowability affirms that reality is orderly and accessible to human understanding; it does not claim omniscience over every contingent physical detail or future event.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: On this account, whatever is called knowledge must become intelligible within the knower, directive in practical action, verifiable in relationships and nature, communicable to fellow humans, and in perfect harmony with the coexistence it reveals.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2. The Advaita Vedanta Answer

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta gives two answers to the question of the knower, and comparison becomes distorted if they are collapsed. Within empirical life (vyavahara), an embodied person cognizes through perception, inference, testimony, and the other accepted means of knowledge. From the absolute standpoint (paramartha), the witnessing Self is not one individual knower among others: it is non-dual consciousness, identical with Brahman, in which the distinction between knower, known, and knowing does not finally apply. The world is consequently valid for empirical cognition while remaining mithya, dependent rather than independently absolute.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.1 Empirical knower and witnessing consciousness

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Classical Indian epistemology analyses a cognition through a subject or knower (pramatr), a means of knowledge (pramana), an object (prameya), and the resulting valid cognition (prama). Advaita accepts this structure at the empirical level. The embodied jiva, equipped with body, senses, and the internal organ (antahkarana), is the person who sees, infers, remembers, deliberates, and acts. Ahamkara, the appropriating “I”-notion, is one function in this empirical complex; it is not simply a synonym for the whole jiva.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Later Advaita manuals commonly describe cognition through a modification of the internal organ (antahkarana-vritti) that takes the form of an object and is illumined by consciousness reflected in the mind (chidabhasa). The actionless witness (sakshin) does not perform an epistemic operation alongside perception or inference. It is that by whose presence the changing cognitions of the empirical subject are manifest. The seer–seen discrimination makes this distinction vivid: whatever can itself be observed cannot be the final witness.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “The form1… is perceived and the eye… is its perceiver… It… is perceived and the mind… is its perceiver. The mind with… modifications is perceived and the Witness (the Self) is verily the perceiver… But… is not perceived…” — DDV, p. 15

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The physical body, senses, emotions, and thoughts are all available as objects of awareness; Advaita therefore denies that any one of them is the ultimate seer. Bhagavad Gita 13.1–3 distinguishes the body as “field” from its knower and then identifies the one knower in all fields. At the empirical level, however, different persons remain accountable agents and knowers. The text does not license replacing every ordinary act of knowing with an actionless transcendental observer.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Mandukya Upanishad (MU, vv. 3–7) analyses waking, dream, and deep sleep before indicating turiya. Deep sleep is not simply a blank witnessed as another object: prajna is described as undifferentiated, a mass of consciousness and a causal condition in which distinct objects are not cognized, while ignorance remains. Turiya is neither an additional experiential state nor the deep-sleep condition; it is the non-dual Self that is not exhausted by any of the three.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The five-sheath analysis associated with the Taittiriya Upanishad (TU, 2.1–2.5), and developed explicitly as a method of discrimination in later works such as the Vivekachudamani (VC, vv. 154–212), similarly refuses to identify the Self with food-body, vitality, mind, intellect, or causal bliss. Madhyasth Darshan reuses some of the same kosha vocabulary but assigns it a different role: its layers are activities and powers of an enduring jeevan to be understood in awakened participation, not coverings whose discrimination culminates in the unreality of individual separateness (The Ontology of Coexistence §5.7.2).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.2 Empirical knowledge and liberating knowledge

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita does not reduce every instance of knowledge to mystical realization. Perceptual and inferential cognitions can be valid within empirical life: a person may know a pot, a medical fact, or another person’s testimony without thereby knowing Brahman. Liberating knowledge (brahma-jnana) is different in scope. It removes the basic superimposition by which the non-objectifiable Self is taken to be a limited body-mind and reveals the identity indicated by the Upanishadic great sayings.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite.” — TU, 2.1.1

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Taittiriya expression satyam jnanam anantam brahma describes Brahman as reality, consciousness or knowledge, and infinitude. It should not be presented as though the Upanishadic sentence were itself the later compact formula Sat-Chit-Ananda. Advaita receives that later formula as a convergent characterization: not three properties added to a substance, but indications of partless reality as existence, consciousness, and fullness. Consciousness is self-revealing (svaprakasha); it is not known by a second consciousness, which would generate an infinite regress.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “By that alone he comes to know his own Self as Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute and becomes happy.” — VC, v. 152

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Ordinary knowledge preserves the knower–means–known relation. Liberating knowledge removes the ignorance that made this relation appear finally independent. Brahman is consequently not a supreme object known by a surviving individual subject, nor an “absolute knower-known ground” in which both terms retain their ordinary meanings. At paramartha, the relational triad no longer applies.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.3 Error, sublation, and levels of reality

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Shankara opens the Brahma Sutra Bhashya by diagnosing mutual superimposition (adhyasa): the properties of body and mind are attributed to the Self, while consciousness and selfhood are attributed to the body-mind complex. Ordinary perceptual error, such as mistaking a rope for a snake, illustrates correction by sublation (badha): what appeared is cancelled by a cognition that discloses its substrate. Later Advaita develops this into the technical account of mithya as neither independently real nor sheer non-being.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The familiar three-level scheme is a useful later systematization rather than a single doctrine laid out as a table by Shankara. It distinguishes private or apparent error (pratibhasika), shared empirical order (vyavaharika), and the non-dual absolute (paramarthika).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Level What is known? Status of error Apparent (pratibhasika) Rope-snake, dream objects, private errors Sublated by waking or correction Empirical (vyavahara) Bodies, minds, Ishvara, causes, duties, scriptures, science Shared, law-governed; operationally valid; sublated only by brahma-jnana Absolute (paramartha) Brahman, not as an object opposed to a subject Knower–known plurality is sublated

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At vyavahara, the world is not unreal in the way a hallucination is. It is the common field in which evidence, error, causal order, duty, and instruction operate. Its dependence is disclosed only relative to Brahman. Madhyasth Darshan rejects this final sublation: error is removable misidentification within a fully real coexistence, not an epistemic condition whose removal cancels the ultimate independence of plurality (§1.5).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.4 The nature of the knower

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At vyavahara, the knower is the embodied jiva: the Self apparently delimited by body, senses, internal organ, ignorance, and agency. This empirical subject is neither identical with ahamkara alone nor dismissed as a hallucination. It is the bearer of responsibility, qualification, inquiry, and liberating instruction so long as ignorance persists. The witness is actionless, but the empirical knower performs cognition and action.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At paramartha, Brahman is one without a second (ekamevaditiyam, CU 6.2.1). Separate knowers cannot therefore be finally independent entities. The language of limiting adjuncts (upadhi), reflection, and superimposition explains how one consciousness appears as many knowers without undergoing real division. These explanatory models are pedagogically related but should not be treated as a single literal mechanism accepted identically by every Advaita author.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Ishvara is Brahman associated with Maya and functions within vyavahara as the omniscient source and governor of ordered name-form manifestation. Advaita commonly treats Ishvara as both material and efficient cause of the empirical universe, not merely an external operative cause and not a creator ex nihilo. The individual jiva is conditioned by individual ignorance; later pedagogical texts distinguish this from cosmic Maya, although terminology varies across authors. Both distinctions cease at paramartha:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “These two are the superimpositions of Ishwara and the Jiva respectively, and when these are perfectly eliminated, there is neither Ishwara nor Jiva.” — VC, v. 244

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Vivekachudamani passage is useful evidence for a later pedagogical presentation, but its attribution to Shankara is disputed. The same caution applies to the Drig-Drishya-Viveka. They illuminate the received Advaita tradition without replacing the Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, and Shankara’s securely attributed commentaries as primary anchors. Full causal and cosmological comparison appears in The Ontology of Coexistence §§2.4–2.5.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.5 The nature of the known

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Empirical objects, persons, space, time, and causal relations are knowable within the shared world. Their empirical validity is not denied whenever one sees or names them correctly. Advaita denies that their differentiated forms possess self-sufficient reality apart from Brahman. CU 6.1.4 presents the clay analogy: transformations are names grounded in speech, while clay is the material reality through which the transformations are understood.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “A firm conviction of the mind to the effect that Brahman is real and the universe unreal, is designated as discrimination (Viveka) between the Real and the unreal.” — VC, v. 20

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “The individual soul is itself and directly the Supreme Brahman, and nothing else.” — VC, v. 216

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The analogy does not make Brahman one more substance among substances. Nor does realization physically destroy the experienced world. It removes the claim that plurality exists independently and absolutely. The liberated person’s continued experience belongs to vyavahara; the non-dual standpoint denies that this field establishes a second reality beside Brahman.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.6 Means of knowledge and liberating instruction

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Later systematic Advaita, represented by works such as Dharmaraja’s Vedanta Paribhasa, normally accepts six means of valid cognition: perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), comparison (upamana), postulation (arthapatti), non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), and verbal testimony (shabda). Earlier Advaita presentations do not always enumerate or analyse them in exactly the same way. This historical qualification matters because the sixfold list is a mature scholastic account, not a verbatim scheme in every foundational text.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The word pramana is also a false friend in this comparison. In Advaita and other classical Indian epistemologies it means an instrument or source that generates valid cognition. In Madhyasth Darshan’s English translations, “evidence” or pramana often names the lived confirmation of realization in conduct, work, participation, and conveyance. The two uses overlap around warrant but are not equivalent.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Means of cognition Empirical competence Limit in Advaita Perception and inference Objects, relations, causal and practical judgments Operate through subject–object distinction Comparison, postulation, non-apprehension Linguistic learning, explanatory entailment, warranted absence Establish empirical cognitions, not non-duality independently Ordinary testimony Knowledge received from competent speakers Remains corrigible within shared life Upanishadic shabda Reveals the otherwise unavailable identity of Self and Brahman Does not turn Brahman into a perceptible object

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: All means of knowledge function for a student within vyavahara. Upanishadic testimony is unique not because it operates as a paramarthika transaction outside duality, but because it removes ignorance about an identity unavailable to perception and inference. Shankara allows that a qualified student may understand the sentence at first hearing. Reflection (manana) removes intellectual doubt, and sustained contemplation (nididhyasana) addresses contrary dispositions or obstacles; they do not manufacture the validity of scripture after it was previously invalid.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The pedagogical discipline is conventionally expressed as hearing, reflection, and contemplation under a qualified teacher:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Shravana — hearing and understanding the Upanishadic teaching.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Manana — reasoning that resolves doubts about the teaching.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Nididhyasana — sustained assimilation where habitual contrary identification remains.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “The Self, my dear Maitreyi, should be realised—should be heard of, reflected on and meditated upon.” — BU, 2.4.5

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: First-person discrimination and neti neti (BU, 2.3.6) work within this teaching by withdrawing mistaken identifications. The comparison with Madhyasth Darshan’s awakened tradition is therefore structural but limited. Both value an accomplished teacher and assimilated understanding; Advaita treats Upanishadic testimony as the decisive means for non-dual Self-knowledge, whereas Madhyasth Darshan asks realization to become publicly legible in humane conduct and successful conveyance (§1.6).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.7 Liberation and complete knowledge

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Liberating knowledge is not acquisition of a new property or merger of a formerly separate substance into Brahman. It is recognition of the identity taught by tat tvam asi, “That thou art” (CU, 6.8.7), through which ignorance of the ever-free Self is removed. BSB 1.1.2 should not be cited as the locus of this identity: it defines Brahman through the origin, continuance, and dissolution of the universe. Shankara’s treatment of Upanishadic identity statements occurs across his commentaries and in the later sections of the Brahma Sutra Bhashya.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “There is neither death nor birth, neither a bound nor a struggling soul, neither a seeker after Liberation nor a liberated one – this is the ultimate truth.” — VC, v. 574

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “The Supreme Brahman is, like the sky, pure, absolute, infinite, motionless and changeless, devoid of interior or exterior, the One Existence, without a second, and is one’s own Self.” — VC, v. 393

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita commonly distinguishes liberation while living (jivanmukti) from the final cessation of embodied appearance (videhamukti). Knowledge removes ignorance; the body-mind may continue through already-fructifying karma (prarabdha) without restoring the knower’s former identification. Accounts differ on the exact explanatory status of prarabdha, but the important comparative point is stable: no eternally separate jiva persists as an independent knower after liberation. Madhyasth Darshan instead holds that each jeevan remains numerically distinct and active in coexistence even when awakened (§1.1).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.8 Ethics, loka-sangraha, and what realization evidences

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita does not treat ethical indifference as evidence of realization. The fourfold qualification (sadhana-catushtaya) requires discrimination, dispassion, disciplined virtues, and desire for liberation; the Bhagavad Gita’s disciplines of action and devotion purify the mind for knowledge. In Shankara’s account, action does not directly produce liberation, because an action cannot create the already existent Self. Ethical and contemplative disciplines prepare the knower, while knowledge removes ignorance.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Bhagavad Gita’s explicit discussion of loka-sangraha, sustaining or protecting the world’s order, occurs at 3.20 and 3.25–26. Shankara allows that one who has no personal end left to gain may nevertheless act for the welfare and guidance of others. BG 3.8 establishes the necessity of prescribed action for the unliberated agent, but it should not carry the whole claim about enlightened social responsibility.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Domain Valid at vyavahara Status at paramartha Ethics and duty Required for qualification and social order (BG 3.8, 3.20, 3.25–26) No separate agent remains with a personal end to achieve World and nature Law-governed, shared, beginningless cosmology Mithya — dependent appearance Individual self Real as embodied jiva under upadhi Identical with Brahman; separateness dispelled Relationships and society Loka-sangraha, ordained action for world-welfare Not ultimately separate from Brahman Time and change Past, present, future, birth and death operationally valid Sublated when timeless Self is known

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s objection is therefore not that Advaita lacks ethical discipline or compassionate exemplars. It is that ethical action has a different epistemic and ontological place. In Madhyasth Darshan, mutually fulfilling conduct is constitutive public evidence of understanding in a perpetually real coexistence. In Advaita, ethical fitness prepares the mind and compassionate action may express freedom, but neither produces Self-knowledge nor makes relationships ultimately independent realities. The dispute concerns what conduct proves and what final weight the world retains.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.9 Scope within Indian epistemology

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita is one major Indian answer, not a proxy for Indian epistemology as a whole. Nyaya defends enduring individual selves, a realist world, and a highly articulated theory of inference and testimony. Mimamsa develops distinctive accounts of linguistic authority and the intrinsic or extrinsic validity of cognition. Buddhist epistemologists analyse perception, inference, momentariness, and no-self without accepting Advaita’s Brahman. A comprehensive cross-Indian comparison would therefore require a separate study. Advaita is retained here because its witness analysis, non-dual absolute, and theory of liberating knowledge create the sharpest contrast with Madhyasth Darshan’s enduring plural knowers in coexistence.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Modern Western philosophy offers no single answer to knowledge, knower, and known. Analytic epistemology asks what turns true belief into knowledge; philosophy of mind disputes whether the knower is wholly physical, emergent, embodied, socially constituted, or grounded in consciousness; phenomenological and perspectival approaches begin from lived experience rather than treating it as an afterthought. Physicalism is influential, but it is a contested philosophical position rather than the unanimous conclusion of analytic philosophy.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.1 What is knowledge?

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Analytic epistemology usually distinguishes propositional knowledge—knowing that something is the case—from knowledge-how, acquaintance, and understanding. The traditional justified-true-belief framework concerns propositional knowledge. Gettier (1963) showed that a belief may be justified and true through epistemic luck without amounting to knowledge, so contemporary accounts add or replace conditions involving reliability, safety, proper function, evidence, or intellectual competence.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Reliabilism locates warrant partly in dependable belief-forming processes rather than only in reasons accessible to reflection (Goldman 1979). Virtue epistemology treats knowledge as a success attributable to the knower’s intellectual competence (Sosa 2007). Social epistemology examines testimony, trust, disagreement, institutions, and epistemic injustice, showing why an isolated individual is not the sole unit of assessment (Fricker 2007; Jarczewski and Riggs 2025). These theories compete; “modern Western epistemology” has no single accepted criterion.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s gyan does not map neatly onto any one of these categories. It includes understanding of coexistence and the human being, realization by the knower, and confirmation in conduct (§§1.1–1.6). Analytic epistemology can ask whether its claims are true, warranted, reliably formed, communicable, and socially responsible, but it will not ordinarily define humane conduct as part of what makes a proposition known. Scientific method, meanwhile, is an institutional way of producing and correcting empirical knowledge; it belongs to §4 rather than serving as the definition of knowledge in analytic epistemology.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.2 Naturalistic accounts of the knower

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Physicalist and naturalistic accounts identify knowing with capacities of embodied organisms or with cognitive processes realized by them (Churchland 1986; Dennett 1991). Some theories reduce mental states to physical or functional states; others treat consciousness and selfhood as emergent, embodied, enacted, or distributed across organism and environment. They agree less about consciousness than the label “naturalism” can suggest.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Many physicalists reject a Cartesian inner observer. On representational accounts, the self is a dynamically maintained self-model integrating perception, memory, bodily regulation, action, and social recognition. Enactive and embodied accounts resist the picture of a brain constructing an inner replica for a detached spectator; they locate cognition in skilled organism–environment engagement. Both differ from an indivisible jeevan, though for different reasons.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: The causal closure of the physical is a philosophical thesis used in arguments for physicalism (Kim 2005), not a separately measured law stating that every event already has a sufficient physical cause. Conservation laws constrain physical quantities, but by themselves do not settle the metaphysics of mind or show that intention would have to “inject energy.” The sharper challenge to Madhyasth Darshan is explanatory: if jeevan is distinct from the body yet affects neural action, the account needs a publicly assessable relation between its activities and measured brain processes. Without such criteria, physicalism remains contestable while jeevan remains empirically underdetermined.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.3 Scientific realism and the scope of the known

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Scientific realism is a philosophical interpretation of successful science: well-confirmed theories aim to describe a mind-independent world, including unobservable entities supported by explanatory and predictive success. Instrumentalists and constructive empiricists grant the practical and empirical success of theories without making the same commitment to their unobservable ontology. Science itself does not decide this dispute by methodological fiat.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: The scientifically investigated world includes physical, biological, psychological, and social phenomena insofar as claims about them can be made publicly answerable to evidence. Public does not mean directly visible or purely quantitative: scientists infer unobservables, use models and instruments, and can treat disciplined first-person reports as data when collection and interpretation are calibrated. Spacetime in physics remains a mathematically articulated dynamical structure, not omnipresent knowledge-energy (The Ontology of Coexistence §4.5; Nature of Time).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan expands the known to include relationship, value, dharma, and humane order as objective dimensions of coexistence (§1.1). Western philosophy contains realist and anti-realist accounts of value, while psychology and social science investigate moral cognition and institutions. Descriptive findings alone do not entail prescriptive conclusions without normative premises. The comparison should therefore oppose neither “physical facts” to “values” nor science to all normativity; it should ask what kind of evidence supports claims that values are features of reality rather than human responses, practices, or constructions.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.4 The hard problem, mystery, and first-person evidence

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Philosophy of mind distinguishes explanatory questions from the analysis of knowledge. Third-person accounts are powerful on mechanism and prediction, yet Chalmers’s hard problem asks why and how physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience (Chalmers 1995; Nagel 1974):

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: “The really hard problem of consciousness is the problem of experience.” — Chalmers 1995, p. 3

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: “the fact that an organism has conscious experience at all means, basically, that there is something it is like to be that organism.” — Nagel 1974, p. 1

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: The argument begins from the reality of experience, but its conclusion is disputed. Reductive physicalists expect a functional or neuroscientific explanation; illusionists argue that the apparently ineffable properties attributed to consciousness are products of introspective representation (Frankish 2016); non-reductive physicalists treat experience as irreducible without making it a separate substance; panpsychists or Russellian monists assign experience or proto-experiential character a fundamental role (Strawson 2006; Goff 2019; Hashemi 2025). These are philosophical positions constrained by science, not established findings of consciousness science.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: The hard problem does not prove an extra-physical jeevan, and neural correlation does not by itself solve the hard problem. Madhyasth Darshan makes a stronger proposal: mystery (rahasyata) is a removable deficit in the knower’s reflection, and disciplined realization can disclose the constitution and activity of the knower (§1.6). Comparative evaluation must therefore ask what such realization predicts, how it is distinguished from introspective error, and how first-person discrimination is coordinated with public evidence.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.5 Error, bias, and epistemic correction

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Western epistemology distinguishes several failures that should not be merged. A belief may be false, accidentally true, irresponsibly held, produced by an unreliable process, distorted by bias, or defeated by evidence the believer ignores. Testimonial injustice and institutional exclusion add social failures that cannot be located only inside an individual’s reasoning. Gettier cases concern epistemic luck even when belief is justified and true; they are not examples of experimental non-replication.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Scientific practices address a subset of these failures through calibration, controls, statistical criticism, replication, adversarial testing, and revision. Phenomenology addresses another subset by examining how objects and selfhood are given in experience; psychotherapy, contemplative disciplines, and moral education address still others. None supplies an infallible correction regime.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan foregrounds false learning, delusion, and contradiction between claimed understanding and conduct (§1.5). Advaita foregrounds superimposition and ignorance of Self (§2.3). Analytic epistemology asks whether belief is warranted and non-accidental, while science asks whether empirical claims survive public tests. The live comparison is not first-person against third-person correction, but how different kinds of error are diagnosed and how their proposed corrections become independently assessable.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.6 Personal identity and brain death

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Physicalism’s answer to post-mortem persistence is typically negative: if personal capacities are realized by a living brain and organism, their irreversible destruction ends the person. Clinical criteria of death serve medical and legal decisions; they are not themselves a complete philosophical theory of personal identity. No reproducible public evidence has established the continued agency of an individual knower after bodily death.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Personal identity theory asks what, if anything, makes a person the same individual over time. Locke tied identity to psychological continuity — memory and connectedness of consciousness — rather than sameness of material particles. Parfit (1984) argued that what matters in survival is psychological connectedness, not a further fact of deep identity beyond the stream of mental states.
