On reductionist readings, the question “is this the same knower after death?” has no fact of the matter beyond causal and psychological links — which bodily death breaks (SEP Personal Identity).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s jeevan (§1.1) and Advaita’s eternal Atman (§§2.4 and 2.7) both reject this outcome on different grounds. Physicalism sets a high evidential bar: without operational criteria for a non-neural knower or independent post-death evidence, immortal jeevan remains a metaphysical posit, while the hard problem (§3.4) exposes the incompleteness of current physical explanation without proving either rival view.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: 3.7 Social, embodied, and perspectival knowing

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Phenomenology begins from intentionality: consciousness is consciousness of something, and objects are disclosed through embodied, temporal, and perspectival experience. Husserl’s suspension of the natural attitude is a methodological refusal to settle metaphysics before describing experience, not the Advaita conclusion that the experienced world is mithya. Merleau-Ponty’s embodied subject is not a detached witness behind the body; bodily orientation is constitutive of perceptual access to a shared world (SEP Phenomenology).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Embodied and enactive approaches carry part of this insight into cognitive science by treating cognition as skilled activity of organism and environment rather than passive construction of an inner picture. Perspectival realism holds that scientific knowledge is historically, instrumentally, and conceptually situated while remaining capable of truth about a mind-independent world (Massimi 2022). These positions give the knower’s standpoint a constructive role without making truth merely private.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-epistemology-and-philosophy-of-mind
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Epistemology and Philosophy of Mind
passages.text: Social epistemology adds that testimony, trust, expertise, institutions, and relations of power affect what people can responsibly know. It comes closer to Madhyasth Darshan’s emphasis on tradition and conveyance, but it evaluates testimonial competence and social conditions rather than presupposing an awakened lineage. The comparison is therefore not exhausted by “matter versus soul.” It also concerns whether knowledge is belief, reliable competence, lived disclosure, social achievement, understanding, or conduct-evidenced realization—and how first-person and public evidence constrain one another.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4. Modern Scientific Approaches

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: The natural sciences operationalise knowledge through observation, measurement, modelling, prediction, experiment, and replication. They do not ordinarily define a metaphysical knower. They investigate organisms, brains, behaviour, reports, and environments, while adopting methodological naturalism: explanations are sought in publicly testable processes rather than in unmeasured sentient units.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.1 Method and means of knowing

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Natural science adopts methodological naturalism: it seeks explanations through publicly testable processes without requiring a prior proof that only natural entities exist. Measurement, formal models, experiment, and institutional criticism extend ordinary perception and inference (Popper 1959). Science can constrain philosophical accounts of mind, but an experimental result does not by itself select a complete metaphysics. SB likewise records that humans seek to live with evidence through experimentation, behaviour, and experience (SB, p. 44); Madhyasth Darshan extends that demand into realization and conduct (The Ontology of Coexistence §4).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: The principal scientific practices do not map one-to-one onto Indian pramana lists, although some functions are comparable:

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Modern source Primary role Limits for mind/self claims Perception (incl. instruments) Data acquisition from world and body Theory-laden; does not directly observe non-physical jeevan Inference and modelling Hypothesis, prediction, mathematical structure Multiple models may fit the same data; ontology requires further argument Measurement and experiment Controlled test of predictions Experiment here means hypothesis-testing and replication — not Madhyasth Darshan’s wider verification in production and lived orderliness (§1.6) Testimony and trust Collective knowledge via experts, records, education Depends on epistemic communities; social virtue epistemology develops this (§3.7) Replication and review Error control across communities Reliability varies by design, incentives, and access to evidence

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Public accountability, rather than a ban on first-person evidence, is the governing standard. Pain ratings, perceptual reports, introspective confidence, and phenomenological interviews can enter research as data, but their elicitation and interpretation must be open to calibration and criticism. First-person experience is indispensable to consciousness research; it is not by itself evidence for immortal units or sufficient warrant for a metaphysical theory.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.2 Brain, organism, and conscious report

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Neuroscience establishes systematic dependence between brain activity and perception, memory, language, decision, and conscious report (Kandel et al. 2021). Injury, stimulation, anaesthesia, development, and degeneration alter the capacities attributed to a knower. These findings support brain-based accounts, but dependence does not by itself settle whether consciousness is identical with neural activity, emerges from it, or accompanies it under a deeper ontology.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan accepts the brain as the body’s enriched signal-processing organ while assigning understanding and evaluation to jeevan (§1.3). The scientific question is whether that distinction predicts anything beyond brain–behaviour models. A viable empirical programme would need operational markers of jeevan, not only philosophical dissatisfaction with physicalism.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.3 Consciousness science and unresolved theory

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Consciousness science contains competing research programmes, including global neuronal workspace, integrated information, higher-order, recurrent-processing, and predictive-processing accounts. Illusionism and panpsychism are broader philosophical interpretations, not programmes of the same experimental kind. Adversarial testing of IIT and GNWT has challenged distinctive predictions of both rather than selecting an uncontested winner (Melloni et al. 2025). This pluralism shows an unfinished explanatory field, not positive evidence for Madhyasth Darshan.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: The hard problem remains the philosophical question of why physical processing should have a first-person aspect at all (§3.4). Experimental science can map neural correlates, behavioural capacities, and report conditions without resolving that metaphysical question. Madhyasth Darshan offers jeevan as its answer, but the existence and interaction of such a unit remain to be independently established.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.4 Error control and public evidence

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Scientific error correction depends on calibrated instruments, statistical discipline, replication, peer review, and adversarial testing. Its strength is that results need not depend on the moral or contemplative attainment of a particular observer. Its limits are equally clear: institutional procedures can reproduce shared assumptions, and third-person measures do not exhaust the first-person character of experience or the normative question of how knowledge should guide conduct.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s evidence chain and scientific replication therefore overlap only partly. Both require claims to face consequence and correction. Science privileges methodologically reproducible observations; Madhyasth Darshan additionally requires coherence among realisation, behaviour, work, relationship, and transmission (§1.6). The latter is broader, but breadth does not automatically supply the controls against suggestion, authority, and confirmation bias that science has developed.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.5 Ethics, value, and life’s purpose

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Evolutionary biology can explain how cooperation, kin concern, punishment, and norm sensitivity developed; psychology and social science investigate empathy, reasoning, institutions, and cultural variation. These are explanations of capacities and practices, not by themselves proofs that a moral norm is true. Philosophical naturalists consequently divide among moral realism, constructivism, contractualism, expressivism, and error theory.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Survival and reproduction describe central consequences of natural selection, not a scientifically prescribed purpose for a human life. Purposes involving relationship, vocation, inquiry, justice, or flourishing require practical and ethical judgment. Science can illuminate their conditions and consequences but does not establish a single cosmic telos of awakening, liberation, or realization in coexistence.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan makes a stronger unity claim: value, humane purpose, knowledge, and conduct belong to the objective order of coexistence and confirm one another (§§1.2 and 1.6). The scientific and philosophical challenge is to show how this normative order is known, how disagreement is corrected, and why successful conduct supports its ontology rather than only its practical usefulness.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.6 Beyond simple brain reduction

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Cognitive science is not restricted to a passive input–computation–output picture. Predictive-processing and active-inference approaches model an organism as anticipating sensory causes and acting to maintain viable states (Limanowski and Blankenburg 2013; Wiese 2024; Tufft et al. 2024). Embodied and enactive research instead emphasizes sensorimotor skill, bodily regulation, and environmental coupling (IEP Enactivism; Piredda 2024). Both make agency more distributed than a brain-only slogan suggests, while remaining compatible with naturalistic investigation.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Research that coordinates careful experiential reports with neural and behavioural measures offers a possible bridge between first-person and public evidence. Such work does not treat introspection as infallible: reports are trained, sampled, compared, and related to independently measured processes. This is methodologically closer to Madhyasth Darshan’s demand that inner realization meet observable consequences, although it does not presuppose jeevan or humane conduct as the ontology and criterion of consciousness.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: These developments leave open whether cognition is best described as representational or enactive, brain-bound or organism–environmental, and reducible or irreducible. They do not remove the principal scientific objection to Madhyasth Darshan: a distinct jeevan has no agreed operational marker that discriminates its contribution from brain–body dynamics.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Public science has established precise mechanism, prediction, and correction across many domains. It has not established immortal jeevan or post-death continuity of a sentient unit (§§1.1 and 7.4). An explanatory gap in consciousness is not an existence proof for jeevan; predictive accuracy alone does not settle whether the regulator is only neural or a distinct unit working through the brain (§7.3).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.1 Key contrasts

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The deepest ontological contrast is between perpetual plurality and non-dual dependence. Madhyasth Darshan holds Space and every material and sentient unit to be real in coexistence: Brahma satya hai, jagat satat hai — Brahma is truth, the world is perpetual (§1.1). Advaita grants the world empirical validity but denies it independent absolute reality. Science investigates a stable public order without, by method alone, deciding between every realist and anti-realist interpretation; it offers no evidence that physical spacetime is omnipresent knowledge.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The accounts of the knower must be compared at matching levels. Advaita’s empirical jiva perceives, reasons, acts, and bears responsibility; the witness is actionless and illumines these activities; at paramartha, no separate knower remains. Madhyasth Darshan’s jeevan remains a distinct active sentient unit in both ignorance and awakening. Naturalistic approaches locate activity in brain, body, environment, and social practice. The contrast is therefore not simply an active knower against a passive one, but enduring plural agency against empirically operative agency whose separateness is finally sublated.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Knowledge and conduct also occupy different logical roles. Madhyasth Darshan places humane conduct within complete knowledge and treats its expression in behaviour, work, relationship, and conveyance as evidence (§§1.1 and 1.6). Advaita requires ethical qualification and permits liberated action for loka-sangraha, but conduct neither produces nor constitutes brahma-jnana. Western virtue and social epistemology connect knowing with competence and responsibility, while natural science evaluates claims through publicly corrigible methods rather than the moral attainment of a claimant.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The four approaches diagnose different primary errors. Madhyasth Darshan identifies incomplete or misdirected activity of jeevan and contradiction between realization and conduct. Advaita identifies superimposition of body-mind and Self, removed by Upanishadic knowledge. Analytic epistemology distinguishes falsehood, luck, unreliable formation, and social distortion; science institutionalizes controls against measurement error, confounding, bias, and failed prediction. A comparative test must ask whether each method can detect the errors to which its own practitioners are vulnerable.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.2 Sat-Chit-Ananda versus distributed coexistence

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita’s Sat-Chit-Ananda and Madhyasth Darshan’s coexistence can sound alike — both speak of being, consciousness, and fulfilment. The contrast is over what those words name and whether the world survives them (The Ontology of Coexistence §5.6).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Concept Advaita Vedanta (unified non-dualism) Madhyasth Darshan (distributed coexistence) Sat (Being) Brahman is independent reality; names and forms have dependent empirical reality. Beingness (astitva) is coexistence of formless Omnipresence and countless real units. Chit (Consciousness) Self-revealing consciousness identical with Self and Brahman; empirical mind and objects are not independently conscious. Omnipresence is pervasive knowledge or condition of intelligibility (§1.1), while active sentience (chaitanya) belongs to each jeevan. The concurrence of atma with Omnipresence in ultimate bliss (§1.2) relates a unit to the ground; it does not dissolve the unit. Ananda (Fullness or bliss) Limitless fullness of Brahman, not a passing mental pleasure. Harmony realized within awakened jeevan and expressed as humane conduct.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Modern philosophy has no parallel formula: it may treat experience as physical, fundamental, or illusory, but it does not name existence as Sat-Chit-Ananda or as coexistence.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3 Partially incommensurable epistemic criteria

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The four approaches do not merely give different answers; they use different criteria for what counts as knowing:

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Tradition Method Adequate for Madhyasth Darshan Study, realization, behaviour, experiment Coexistence as lived evidence; conduct as proof of understanding Advaita Upanishadic testimony, reasoning, and contemplative discrimination (§§2.1–2.7) Valid empirical cognition and removal of ignorance of Self–Brahman identity Modern Western philosophy Argument, experience, justification, reliability, virtue, and social practice (§3) Conceptual warrant and accounts of first- and third-person knowing Natural sciences Observation, modelling, replication, peer review (§4) Mechanism, prediction, and public correction

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: They are partially incommensurable because each includes standards the others do not fully recognise. Comparison can nevertheless test internal consistency, fidelity to experience, fit with public knowledge, explanatory reach, and whether a claimed method controls its own characteristic errors. The remaining disputes are collected in §7.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6. Critical Review

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: No view escapes serious objections. Here is where each is strong and where each is vulnerable.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.1 Madhyasth Darshan — integrated inside, unproven outside

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: It integrates ontology, active selfhood, knowledge, action, value, and social evidence rather than treating epistemology as belief assessment alone.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its linked triads connect perspective, realization, action, result, and evaluation; conduct therefore has genuine epistemic weight (§1.1).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its distinction between cognisance and sensitivity explains why bodily propensities, sensory contact, and social motives require knowledgeable regulation without being rejected.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The knowledge–wisdom–science differentiation connects truth, human purpose, and practical direction, extending that direction to productive and ecological complementarity.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its realism preserves the final significance of nature, individual sentient units, and human relationships.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The claims that Omnipresence is Knowledge and that a constitutionally complete atom is the knower are not independently established by physical measurement.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The argument for the universal availability of knowledge (§1.1) grounds knowability in the equal conscious capacity of all jeevans; however, an equal innate capacity to cognize does not by itself establish that existence is completely knowable without remainder, nor does it guarantee that learners will successfully bridge historical, cultural, or individual obstacles to realization.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its account of vigyan is broader than natural science, but the claims it makes about production, health, ecology, and material process (§§1.1–1.2) remain answerable to physical evidence and are not established by the philosophy itself.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The relation between jeevan and measured brain activity remains underspecified (§7.3).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Conduct-evidence does not yet discriminate Madhyasth Darshan’s ontology from rival paths that also produce resolution or humane action.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The asserted passage from resolved knowledge and just relationship to mutual satisfaction and the four jeevan values needs operational descriptions that can distinguish durable harmony from conformity, self-report, or temporary affect.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The method needs safeguards against circularity when awakening validates the teaching and the teaching identifies awakening, as well as a clearer boundary between structural certitude and corrigible empirical knowledge (§§7.1 and 7.5).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan is best read as an internally integrated epistemology whose decisive tests remain conduct-based and publicly contestable, not as a demonstrated ontology.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.2 Advaita Vedanta — disciplined self-inquiry, disputed non-duality

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita distinguishes ordinary cognition from the consciousness in whose presence cognition is manifest, preventing a simple identification of the knower with any passing mental state.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its analysis of superimposition explains how bodily, affective, and cognitive predicates become fused with the sense of self.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its account of empirical pramanas, qualified instruction, reasoning, and contemplation is more epistemically articulated than a generic appeal to mystical experience.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Ethical discipline and loka-sangraha answer the claim that non-duality simply licenses withdrawal from empirical responsibility.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Its move from the non-objectifiability of witnessing consciousness to identity with Brahman requires Upanishadic testimony and interpretive argument; introspection alone does not establish cosmic non-duality.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The relation of beginningless ignorance to non-dual Brahman remains contested. Calling avidya dependent and neither absolutely real nor sheer non-being protects non-duality, but critics can still ask whether this explains the appearance of plurality or restates its anomalous status.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The empirical validity of suffering, duty, and relationship supports serious ethics, yet their final sublation gives them a different ontological standing from the perpetual relations asserted by Madhyasth Darshan.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Later Advaita models of jiva, reflection, Maya, and levels of reality are not uniform; comparison must not treat one scholastic formulation as the uncontested view of the entire tradition.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita offers a rigorous account of liberating Self-knowledge when its empirical and absolute levels are kept distinct. Its central comparative vulnerability is not ethical incapacity but the additional argument needed to move from witness analysis to non-dual metaphysics, together with the final dependence it assigns to the plural world.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.3 Modern Western philosophy — plural resources, no settled knower

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Analytic epistemology supplies precise tools for justification, reliability, testimony, intellectual competence, epistemic luck, and social error.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Phenomenology and embodied approaches describe lived and bodily access to the world without reducing experience to an afterthought.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Social epistemology explains why testimony, institutions, trust, and power partly constitute the conditions under which individuals know.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The plurality of approaches can fragment the relation among warranted belief, consciousness, understanding, value, and conduct.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: A theory may explain when a proposition counts as known without explaining the nature of the subject who knows it.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Physicalist, phenomenological, enactive, idealist, and social accounts can share vocabulary while disagreeing about what the knower and known ultimately are.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Modern Western philosophy makes the conceptual alternatives explicit but does not deliver a single replacement for the integrated Madhyasth Darshan triad.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.4 Natural sciences — powerful correction, bounded scope

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Measurement, intervention, prediction, replication, and adversarial testing provide powerful controls against individual conviction being mistaken for public knowledge.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Neuroscience establishes detailed dependencies among brain, body, behaviour, report, and cognitive capacity without requiring premature agreement on a final metaphysics of consciousness.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Public methods enable correction across observers, instruments, cultures, and generations.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The hard problem. Neural dependence and correlation do not yet explain why physical processing has a first-person aspect (§§3.4 and 4.3).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: First-person calibration. Reports and experiential descriptions can enter science, but their public calibration may omit aspects of experience that are difficult to operationalize; no agreed method fully coordinates phenomenological structure with neural explanation (§§3.4 and 4.1).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Normative limitation. Descriptive success does not by itself establish justice, humane purpose, or the values by which knowledge should be used (§4.5).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Theory competition. Consciousness science has several live but competing programmes and no settled account of the knower (§4.3).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The natural sciences offer the strongest method for public correction, but the claim that their current ontology is the complete account of knowledge and the knower remains philosophical rather than an experimental result.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.1 Holistic knowability versus fallibilism

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that the structure of coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct can be understood without ontological mystery (§1.6). It does not follow that an awakened person knows every contingent fact. The system needs a clearer account of which claims are held with final certitude, which remain open to empirical correction, and how mistaken certainty would be diagnosed from within the method.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.2 Conduct-evidence and public testability

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Realisation, authenticity, behaviour, experiment, and transmission form Madhyasth Darshan’s evidence regime (§1.6). Science requires operational and reproducible discrimination among competing explanations. Public evaluation of jeevan would require at minimum:

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Operational criteria for constitutional completeness independent of the philosophy.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Reproducible markers distinguishing jeevan-mediated from brain-only activity.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Independent evidence for post-death continuity of a sentient unit.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Until then, immortal jeevan remains a metaphysical commitment not validated by current science. Realisation as pramana is an epistemic criterion, not itself a metaphysical entity; the open question is whether its conduct and transmission tests can distinguish Madhyasth Darshan’s ontology from rival paths that also produce resolution or ethical conduct. The explanatory gap in consciousness is not by itself evidence for jeevan.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.3 Jeevan–body interaction and physical causation

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: If jeevan coordinates the body through the joint form (§1.3), either it makes a measurable difference to neural activity or “driving” names a non-mechanical relation that still requires specification. The texts’ signal language is more precise than a crude Cartesian push, but it does not yet answer the closure-based objection or show what observations would differ if jeevan were absent.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.4 Post-death continuity as inference, not measurement

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Post-death continuity of jeevan is inferred from its constitutional completeness (gathan-purnata)—the stable atomic constitution that neither admits nor expels constituent particles, rendering it free from molecular decomposition and weight-bondage (§§1.1–1.2). While internally consistent, this continuity is an inferential deduction rather than a third-person empirical measurement. Showing that an atomic structure ceases to exchange particles does not by itself empirically demonstrate that individual conscious memory, desire, or agency persists without biological substrate. Madhyasth Darshan’s account of freedom from weight-bondage (bhaar-bandhan-mukti) and molecular-bondage (anu-bandhan-mukti) must therefore carry the argument, remaining an open point of contact with physics, mereology, and neuroscience (The Ontology of Coexistence §6.2.3).

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.5 Teacher, tradition, and circular validation

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan requires guidance from a realised human and treats successful conveyance as evidence (§1.6). This creates a productive second-person discipline but also a circularity risk: the teacher may be recognised as realised through the doctrine, while the doctrine is trusted through the teacher. The tradition needs explicit safeguards for disagreement, failed transmission, authority error, and correction of a respected teacher.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.6 Non-substitutable evidence across domains

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: The darshan expects coherence across realisation, thought, relationship, work, result, and social participation (§1.6). Admirable conduct does not thereby prove every ontological assertion by scientific standards: a person may behave well while holding a mistaken cosmology, and a successful production method may not verify the proposed constitution of jeevan. Conduct-evidence is strongest for claims about resolution, relationship, and humane participation, while claims about physical process, neural causation, or post-death continuity require domain-appropriate public tests (§§7.2–7.4). The darshan does not yet state a public rule for cases in which the domains diverge: sound conduct with disputed metaphysics, contemplative certitude with failed prediction, or successful production with unjust relationships. The evidence framework in From Unit Activity to Human Orderliness §12.6 and Appendix C suggests the right discipline — success in one domain must not silently substitute for failure in another — but the criteria for adjudicating such mixed cases remain to be developed in ordinary prose and practice.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: 7.7 From regulation to jeevan values

passages.heading: 7-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan-epistemology
passages.section: 7. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan epistemology
passages.text: The primary texts give a strong conceptual bridge from knowledge through regulation and just relationship to happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss (§§1.2 and 1.4). They give less detail about how an observer or community should assess that bridge in difficult cases. A practical epistemology still needs criteria for distinguishing restraint from repression, prosperity from accumulation, public participation from reputation-seeking, beneficence from dependency-making, mutual satisfaction from mere agreement, and stable faculty-harmony from temporary positive affect. It also needs an account of cases in which correct intention and competent effort meet refusal, material scarcity, illness, or conflict beyond one person’s control. These questions do not negate the value structure; they identify the next work required to make its claimed evidence intersubjectively discriminating.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: 8. Conclusion

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s distinctive contribution to comparative epistemology is not merely an additional definition of knowledge. It joins the intelligibility of coexistence, jeevan as the active knower, humane conduct as part of what must be known, and the consequences of action as evidence that returns to the knower. Because the human being is a unit of the knowledge order whose dharma is happiness, this understanding must govern bodily propensities, sensory engagement, social motives, relationship, production, and participation in nature. Knowledge, knower, and known become complete together when knowledge, wisdom, and science are stable across realisation, thought, relationship, work, evaluation, and transmission. This gives epistemology an ethical, ecological, and civilisational reach that neither belief-centred analysis nor mechanism-centred science ordinarily claims.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: The comparison also fixes the limits of that contribution. Advaita offers a more radical account of the witness by dissolving the triad at the highest level; Madhyasth Darshan preserves the distinction and participation of real units within coexistence. Modern Western philosophy provides plural accounts of warrant, embodiment, first-person experience, and social knowledge. Natural science supplies the strongest available procedures for public correction and causal explanation. Madhyasth Darshan must therefore show how realisation and conduct-evidence control error without circularity, and how claims about jeevan differ observationally from biological accounts.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: The primary texts thus support a layered epistemic structure. Knowledge has coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct as its canonical contents; it governs bodily propensities through sensory engagement, resolution and the three eshanas in social life, and upakar as higher-human participation. Deliberation considers pleasantness, bodily well-being, and material gain under the governing perspectives of justice, dharma, and truth, while law, regulation, and balance connect understanding to orderly activity. Knowing and accepting continue through recognition, fulfilment, result, evaluation, correction, and transmission. This structure explains the framework’s coherence without removing its open problems: its claims still require clearer public tests, intersubjective safeguards, and dialogue with the sciences.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Key terms from §§1–4 are collected here for quick reference. Most are defined where they first appear; the glossary also preserves compact technical structures that the exposition does not develop at length.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §1

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Coexistence (saha-astitva) Reality as the pervasive ground (satta) and all units (ikai) inseparably present together. Astitva Darshan Gyan Knowledge of existence as coexistence of Omnipresence (vyapak satta) and units (ikai) across four orders (§1.1). Jeevan Gyan Knowledge of the conscious unit (jeevan), its faculties, ten activities, and potential for awakening (§1.1). Manaviyata Purna Acharan Gyan Knowledge of humane conduct, including values, character, ethics, and universal orderliness (§1.1). Vastugat Satya Objective / inherent truth: the reality of each unit’s form (roop), properties (guna), essential nature (svabhav), and dharma (§1.1). Vastu-sthiti Satya Positional / relational truth: units in space, time, direction, orderliness, and mutual complementariness (§1.1). Sthiti Satya Existential truth: nature (sentient and insentient units) saturated in all-pervasive Omnipresence (vyapak satta), which is coexistence itself, unaffected by time (§1.1). Anubhav jnan (Realisation Knowledge) Saturated insentient and sentient nature, whose units have form, properties, essential nature, dharma, and orderliness (MVD, p. 11; §1.1). Gyan udghatan The unfolding of knowledge through awakened humans or the sentient aspect, not cognition performed by Omnipresence (§1.1). Samadhan (Resolution) Realised knowledge established as freedom from contradiction, with correct answers to why and how for activity; also grouped with the three eshanas in intellectual satisfaction (§§1.2 and 1.4). Gyan–vivek–vigyan Knowledge of coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct; wisdom that recognises the human goal; and science that determines direction for material prosperity and the human and jeevan goals (§1.2). Knowledge–knower–known Knowledge of coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct; jeevan as bearer of knowing; coexistence as object made meaningful in awakened living (§1.1). Darshan–drish–drishya / drishti Darshan is assigned to justice, dharma, and truth, drish to human jeevan, and drishya to coexistence; awakened jeevan is the seer and darshan the meaningful exposition. Drishti names perspective (KD §3.17, pp. 145–150; MVD, p. 84; §1.1). Dhyan–dhyata–dhyeya The attention structure: awakening, the human attender, and freedom from delusion together with the jeevan values and evidence of the human goal (KD §3.17, pp. 145–150; §1.1). Karan–karta–karya Cause–doer–effect at two levels: knowledge-state–human–universal participation, and coexistence–jeevan–awakened human status (KD §3.17, pp. 145–150; §1.1). Sadhya–sadhak–sadhan Awakening or seer-status as aim, the human being as seeker, and body together with jeevan as means; tradition, imagination, and freedom of action support those means (KD §3.17, pp. 145–150; §1.1). Sapekshata (Relativity) Differentiation among perspective, observed scene, and worldview; in this context, the changing relativity of sensory, bodily, and material criteria rather than unreality of coexistence (§1.4). Six evaluative perspectives Priya–apriya concerns sensory pleasantness, hita–ahita bodily well-being, labha–alabha material gain, nyaya–anyaya relationship and behaviour, dharma–adharma resolution and orderly participation, and satya–asatya realisation in existence (§1.4). Five forces / five powers The ten activities divided as force and power: five activities of state expressed as force and five of motion expressed as power, the projected five appearing as hope, thought, desire, truth-resolve (ritambhara), and authenticity (KD §3.6, pp. 70–71; KD §3.16, p. 145; §1.3). Madhyasthata (Mediativeness) The central, non-partisan situation of atma by which the mediative activity attains the touch of knowledge in every dimension, evidenced only through integrality of behaviour and thought (MVD, p. 211; §1.3). Purvanukram / *Paranukram* Higher-conformance (purvanukram, पूर्वानुक्रम): governance of mun by inspiration from vritti, chitta, buddhi, and atma, aligned with justice. Lower-conformance (paranukram, परानुक्रम): pressure from prana, senses, body, and conditioning (MVD, pp. 207–208; §1.3). Manah-swasthata (Mental well-being) The realisation of happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss in the state of higher-conformance (MVD, p. 208; §1.2). Sanvedansheelta / *sangyansheelta* Sensitivity through the body and senses, and cognisance through jeevan’s knowing and accepting. Cognisance regulates sensitivity (§1.3). Four vishayas Food, rest, defense, and procreation: bodily propensities retained in the human joint form and regulated rather than treated as the source of jeevan’s happiness (§1.4). Five sensory modalities Sound, touch, visible form, taste, and smell: bodily interfaces through which the four vishayas are engaged (§1.4; Editorial Notes). Three eshanas Progeny, wealth, and public-recognition motives, defined through family and society, prosperity and right use, and undivided society or universal orderliness (§1.4). Niyam–niyantran–santulan Law protecting and disciplining activity, regulation according to law, and the balance it sustains; connected to justice, dharma, and truth as a functional progression (§1.4; Editorial Notes). Nyaya / *ubhay-trupti* Justice as relationship-recognition, value-fulfilment, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction, of which mutual satisfaction is the relational outcome (§§1.4–1.5; Editorial Notes). Humane conduct (value, character, ethics) The third content of knowledge: relationship value with evaluation and mutual satisfaction; character as fidelity and compassionate conduct; ethics as protection and right use of body, mind, and wealth (KD §3.4, p. 67; MVD, p. 35; §§1.1 and 1.4). Janna–maanna–pahachanna–nirvaha The integrated fourfold cognitive-action progression: knowing, accepting, recognizing, and fulfilling (§1.5). Ati-, av-, mithya-mulyankan Over-evaluation, under-evaluation, and mis-evaluation of objects, relationships, fulfilment, or results (§1.5). Samyak-mulyankan Right / accurate evaluation of capacity, relationship, and result as they truly are (§1.5). Upakar (Beneficence) Help and inspiration for prosperity and awakening, as the higher-human application of resolved capacity (§1.4; Editorial Notes). Pramana Means or proof of valid knowledge; in Madhyasth Darshan, realization (anubhav) evidenced in living conduct is the ultimate proof (§1.6). Tri-vidha Pramana Threefold evidence: experiential (anubhavatmak), behavioral (vyavaharatmak), and experimental/practical (prayogatmak) (§1.6). Pramanikta (Authenticity) The realisation-bearing activity of atma that becomes publicly evident through conduct, teaching, and humane tradition (§1.6). Pratyaksha–anuman–agama Apprehension through direct perception (realization of continuous proximity), inference (recognizing the possibility of continuity), and testimony-activity (agama-kriya, apprehending existence beyond immediate proximity) (KD, pp. 20–21; §1.6). Adhyayan / Abhyas Systematic study through proposal (prastav), hearing (shravan), reflection (manan), and threefold practice (shastra-abhyas, vyavahara-abhyas, karma-abhyas) (MVD, pp. 88, 143–144; §1.6). Anubhav-gami / anubhav-mulak bodh Realization-oriented understanding (the learner’s understanding accepted in buddhi following direct recognition in chitta through realization-oriented study) and realization-based understanding (the awakened stage where realization in atma guides all thought and living) (MVD, pp. 98–99; §1.6). Sahaj Swikriti (Natural Acceptance) Here, the aspiration toward understanding and harmonious living that motivates inquiry. The proposal is examined through reasoning, practice, and evidence (MVD, p. 88; §1.6 and Editorial Notes). Pratyavartan / Paravartan Inward reflection toward realization, and outward projection into thought, speech, behavior, and work (§1.3). Gathan-, kriya-, acharan-purnata The three completions: constitutional completeness (jeevan, non-decaying atomic constitution with no addition or loss of particles), activity completeness (awakening of all ten activities), and conduct completeness (living evidence in values, character, and ethics) (JV, p. 36; §1.2). Ritambhara Truth-bearing resolve (sankalpa) at buddhi, projecting existential understanding into living (§1.3). Seer–doer–enjoyer Understanding, action, and fruition unified in the awakened human joint form (KD §3.18, pp. 151–152; §1.1). Bhram Delusion — living by inherited belief rather than understanding, rooted in identifying jeevan with the body. Rahasyata (Mysteriousness) Incapacity to attain, evidence, or impart complete understanding (§1.6). Bauddhik rahasyata (Intellectual mystery) Internal misalignment and contradiction among the faculties of jeevan (mun not in refuge of vritti, vritti not in chitta, chitta not in buddhi), resolved through exploration and study (MVD, pp. 279–282; §1.6). Anushandhan (Exploration) Inventive comprehensive study from decline through development and awakening to Omnipresence (MVD, Ch. 17; §1.6). Jeevan The sentient self — in Shri Nagraj’s view a real, eternal, atom-scale entity that works through the body. Ontology: The Ontology of Coexistence. Drishta-pad (Seer status) The unique capacity of the human being in existence to observe, understand, and evaluate all orders of nature (§1.1). Human dharma Happiness as the inseparable human aspiration; knowledge is required to understand and live the law by which happiness is realised (§1.2). Sanskar-anushangita Conformance to understanding and sanskar, the distinctive law of the human knowledge order (§1.2). Human aspiration Resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence at person, family, society, and universal-order scales (§1.2). Jeevan aspiration Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss as harmonies of jeevan; Supreme Bliss (paramanand) in concurrence with Omnipresence (MVD, pp. 208, 327; §1.2).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §2

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Atman / *Brahman* In Advaita Vedanta: the innermost Self / the one ultimate, non-dual reality. Pramatr–pramana–prameya–prama Empirical knower, means of valid cognition, known object, and resulting valid cognition; this structure operates at vyavahara (§§2.1 and 2.6). Jiva The embodied empirical knower and agent under ignorance; its apparent separateness is sublated in liberating knowledge. Sakshin The actionless witnessing consciousness that illumines changing cognitions without becoming another empirical cognitive instrument. Sat-Chit-Ananda A later compact Advaita expression for Brahman as existence, consciousness, and limitless fullness; related to but not identical with TU 2.1.1’s wording. Chit Advaita: consciousness as the very nature of Brahman and the inner Self. Svaprakasha Advaita: consciousness self-luminous — reveals itself without another knower (§2.2). Badha (Sublation) Cancellation of a cognition or claim to independent reality by a cognition with greater authority (§2.3). Mithya Dependent empirical reality: neither independently absolute nor sheer non-being. Moksha Advaita: liberation as recognition of pre-existing identity with Brahman (§2.7).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §3

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Scientific realism The view that successful scientific theories aim to describe a mind-independent world, including well-supported unobservable entities (§3.3). Hard Problem Why physical brain processes are accompanied by subjective experience — a modern open question, not the same as Madhyasth Darshan’s rahasyata (§1.6; §3.4).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §4

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Methodological naturalism The scientific policy of seeking publicly testable natural explanations without assuming that current physicalism is complete. Replication Independent repetition of a method or test as a control on error and investigator-specific conviction (§4.4). Neural correlate A brain state or process systematically associated with a conscious capacity or report; correlation alone does not decide metaphysical identity (§4.2).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The contents of complete knowledge

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Complete knowledge is enumerated with four constituents at KD §3.5, p. 69 — existence as coexistence, jeevan, humane conduct, and participation in overall orderliness — and with three at KD, p. 30, KD §3.17, p. 148, and JV, p. 40, where participation is not listed separately. This study presents the three primary domains and treats participation as the living field in which all three are manifest and evidenced, rather than as an isolated fourth object of knowledge. Nothing in the exposition of §1 depends on which enumeration is preferred.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The Threefold Truth (Vastugat, Vastu-sthiti, Sthiti Satya)

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The definitions of the three truths follow the official Hindi compilation Yatharthata, Vastavikta, Satyata (YAT), under the headings “स्थिति सत्य,” “वस्तुगत सत्य,” and “वस्तु स्थिति सत्य.” The page attributes its excerpts to Paribhasha Sanhita and other writings. Sthiti Satya is existential reality unaffected by time: nature saturated in all-pervasive Omnipresence. Vastugat Satya is the inherent reality of each unit’s form, properties, essential nature, and dharma. Vastu-sthiti Satya concerns direction, time, and place. The ecological and mutual-complementarity explanation in §1.1 places this positional definition within the account of coexistence (SB, pp. 111, 121, 149). MVD pp. 88 and 97 provide connected support for how these truths are studied, understood, and realized.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The Study Methodology and Natural Acceptance

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The transition from delusion to awakening is structured through three broad phases: study (adhyayan), experiment and practice (prayog and abhyas), and realization with evidence (anubhav-praman) (MVD, p. 88). Primary texts distinguish realization-oriented understanding (anubhav-gami bodh), where a student reflects on the proposal and attains direct recognition (sakshatkar) and acceptance in buddhi, from realization-based understanding (anubhav-mulak bodh), where realization in atma directs subsequent resolve, contemplation, thought, and conduct (MVD, pp. 98–99; KD, pp. 112–113). Practice is threefold: literature-practice (shastra-abhyas), behavior-practice (vyavahara-abhyas), and work-practice (karma-abhyas) (MVD, pp. 143–144). This study uses “Natural Acceptance” (sahaj swikriti) as an explanatory phrase for the human aspiration toward understanding and harmonious living, taking the universal thirst for understanding in MVD p. 88 as the starting point for inquiry. It does not introduce an additional source of proof alongside realization, behavior, and experiment; the learner examines the proposal through reasoning, practice, and evidence (§1.6).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Fields of conduct and the contents of knowledge

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The four vishayas, the five sensory modalities, the three eshanas, and upakar identify where knowledge of humane conduct becomes operational (§1.4). They are not further objects of knowledge on the level of coexistence and jeevan, and the four propensities and five modalities are not nine independent activities: the four name the propensity being served, the five the mode of bodily contact through which it is engaged. Upakar is likewise not a fourth eshana, and mutual satisfaction (ubhay-trupti) is the relational outcome of justice rather than a fifth jeevan value.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: “Five sensory modalities” rather than “five samvedanas“

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Samvedana is used broadly in the sources for sensing, for knowledge of the cognitive and work organs, and for a tendency toward development (MVD, p. 313). No stable five-member category of samvedanas parallels the four vishayas, so this study uses “five sensory modalities” as its running term for sound, touch, visible form, taste, and smell (MVD, p. 65).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Niyam–niyantran–santulan and nyaya–dharma–satya

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The sequence at MVD, p. 174 runs from knowledge through law, regulation, and balance to justice, dharma, and truth, while MVD, p. 137 states that behaviour is regulated through justice, thought is disciplined through dharma, realisation occurs through truth, and regulation proceeds through law. This study reads the relation between the two triads as a functional progression, not as three term-by-term equations of niyam with nyaya, niyantran with dharma, and santulan with satya (§1.4).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Seer in the two triads

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Drish in darshan–drish–drishya (KD §3.17, pp. 145–150) names the seeing capacity of human jeevan; the seer in seer–doer–enjoyer (KD §3.18, pp. 151–152) names established seer-status (drishta-pad). The study keeps the two senses distinct (§1.1).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The receptive activity of chitta

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The receptive activity of chitta appears both as contemplation and as direct recognition (sakshatkar). Both name the recognition and formation of meaning rather than bodily sensation, and this study uses “direct recognition” where the contrast with sensory contact is at issue (§1.3).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Attribution of sources

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Section 1 states the darshan’s own positions in continuous prose, with page-level attribution carried in the parenthetical citations and collected by section in the References below. Where this study has chosen among source formulations or supplied a reading the texts do not state in those words, the choice is recorded in these notes rather than in the exposition. Comparison with other traditions is confined to §§2–5, and critical assessment to §§6–7.
